clue.text: The Mock Turtle's first study — swimming

definitions.meaning: in Alice in Wonderland the Mock Turtle says lessons began with ... and Writhing, a pun on reading and writing
as a head can be said to be swimming, giddy and spinning

explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's Mock Turtle names this as the first school subject; a dizzy, spinning head is also described this way.

clue.text: The fruit in Queen Sophie's salad

parts.note: R for Regina, Latin for queen

indicators.note: a salad is a mixture, so the letters are tossed together

parts.note: the name Sophie, the possessive adding nothing

explanation.surface: A berry turns up in the dish prepared by Queen Sophie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salad' mixes R (Regina, queen) with SOPHIE.
explanation.definitionFit: The red seed pod of a wild rose bush, used for syrup.

clue.text: They are used to knock the tops off shells

definitions.text: They are used to knock the tops off shells

parts.words: They are used to knock the tops off shells
parts.note: breakfast utensils for tapping open a boiled egg, not military shells

explanation.definitionFit: Small breakfast utensils for scooping a boiled egg once its top is cracked.

clue.text: Idol, most typical when spitting

definitions.meaning: a statue or likeness worshipped as a god
a spitting likeness is an exact, typical copy

explanation.surface: A pop idol at their most characteristic when spitting.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is a carved likeness; the spitting likeness is the exact double.

clue.text: What a gaudy pub for Geneva bishop's residence!

parts.note: geneva is an old name for gin, from Dutch genever
a bishop lives in a palace

explanation.surface: Exclaiming that a Swiss bishop's house is as garish as a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Geneva' looks like the Swiss city but is an old word for gin.
explanation.definitionFit: A showy Victorian drinking house, flashy and brightly lit.

clue.text: The Master of the Buckhounds is in contempt: twice

definitions.note: one of the many offices held by a character in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado

parts.note: pooh is an exclamation of contempt
bah is a second exclamation of contempt, the 'twice' of the clue

explanation.surface: A royal huntsman finds himself held in contempt of court, not once but two times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twice' asks for two different exclamations of contempt side by side. In Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado this pompous official holds every office going, Master of the Buckhounds among them.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Mikado the Lord High Everything Else lists Master of the Buckhounds among his many posts.

clue.text: Write to the church for Peter's contribution

parts.note: to pen is to write
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Write to the parish asking for a donation.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter's pence was a yearly tax paid to the Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter's pence was the medieval annual payment to Rome, coins given in tribute.

clue.text: Bound to be able to dig anyway

indicators.note: anyway suggests the letters can go in any order they like

explanation.surface: Obliged to be capable of digging, whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges ABLE TO DIG.
explanation.definitionFit: Bound in the sense of under a duty, required to do something.

clue.text: Name to occur to viscount

parts.note: to be is to exist or occur

explanation.surface: A title comes to mind for a nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: Bevis is a male forename, as in the medieval romance Bevis of Hampton.
explanation.definitionFit: A male forename, borne by the hero of a medieval romance.

clue.text: Cushion has covering for feet

parts.note: a sock covers a foot

explanation.surface: A footstool cushion with a cover for the feet.
explanation.walkthrough: A hassock is a kneeling cushion in church.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm padded footstool or kneeler used in church.

clue.text: Old character in disgrace, having lost temper initially

indicators.note: having lost tells us a letter is dropped from the word for disgrace

parts.note: a stigma is a mark of disgrace

indicators.note: initially means take only the opening letter of the word temper

explanation.surface: An old-timer in disgrace after once losing their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old character' is a letter of the ancient Greek alphabet, not an elderly person.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek alphabet's eighteenth letter, an ancient written symbol.

clue.text: One over the eight is Tom's ration

definitions.text: One over the eight is Tom's ration

parts.words: One over the eight is Tom's ration
parts.note: one more than eight is the number that follows it, and a tomcat's ration of existences, by the proverb, is that many

explanation.walkthrough: 'One over the eight' is British slang for one drink too many, which leads away from simple arithmetic; Tom is a tomcat.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb grants a cat that many lives, one more than eight.

clue.text: The hyena could be circling softly — make a dash for it

indicators.note: circling means the rearranged letters go around the piece for softly
could be suggests the letters of the hyena might be rearranged into something else

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical abbreviation for softly

explanation.surface: A hyena, quietly circling its prey, suddenly bolts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges THE HYENA into HYHENATE, and 'circling' puts P inside it. 'make a dash for it' means join words with a hyphen, not run away.
explanation.definitionFit: To join words with a short horizontal stroke between them, a punctuation dash.

clue.text: Emperor reduced to making relish

annotationWithheld.why: Emperor reduced to making relish: no shortening of an emperor's name (AUGUSTUS gives GUST) yields GUSTO, and the remaining words supply no O

clue.text: Doggy bag, no longer posh and nothing in it

indicators.note: no longer, followed by 'and ... in it', signals one letter swapped out for another

parts.note: a pouch is a small bag
U stands for upper-class, hence posh
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A doggy bag from a restaurant that is no longer smart and holds nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no longer posh and nothing in it' tells you to remove U (upper-class, posh) from POUCH and put O (nothing) in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet dog, informally a mutt or hound.

clue.text: Thank you from him, and from me, for the chemical

parts.note: something from him is his
ta is British informal thanks
something from me is mine

explanation.surface: Two people thanking each other for a chemical compound.
explanation.walkthrough: TA is everyday British for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: A compound released in allergic reactions, a body chemical.

clue.text: In a street crowd we get frightened

indicators.note: In places the word we inside a and the street abbreviation

parts.note: a ruck is a crowd or jostling throng

explanation.surface: Caught in a jostling street crowd, we are scared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts the clue's own 'we' between A and the street abbreviation; a ruck is a rugby term for a scrum of players, hence a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: Filled with dread and wonder, overwhelmed with fear.

clue.text: Snared — net could be blamed

indicators.note: could be suggests the word net might be rearranged

parts.note: rapped means blamed or criticised, as in rapped over the knuckles

explanation.surface: Caught in a net that might be to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges NET into ENT, followed by RAPPED.
explanation.definitionFit: Caught in a trap, ensnared.

clue.text: A thin clue, perhaps, for unscrupulous

indicators.note: perhaps hints that a thin clue's letters may be reordered

explanation.surface: A setter's flimsy clue might be thought dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges A THIN CLUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Without moral principles, dishonest.

clue.text: Under canvas half-sister becomes demanding

parts.note: under canvas means in a tent, so under gives in

indicators.note: half, attached to sister by a hyphen, asks for just the first three of its six letters

parts.note: a tent is made of canvas

explanation.surface: Camping, a step-sibling grows ever more demanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under canvas' is the idiom for camping, so it is read as in a tent; the half-sibling, cut to its front half by 'half', is pitched between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing and persistent, refusing to take no for an answer.

clue.text: No one can be so narrow-minded, said Donne

definitions.text: No one can be so narrow-minded, said Donne

parts.words: No one can be so narrow-minded, said Donne
parts.note: John Donne wrote that no man is an island; the adjective from island also means narrow-minded

explanation.definitionFit: Island-like, cut off and parochial, as Donne said no man can be.

clue.text: One is far away to have this the day before

definitions.text: One is far away to have this the day before

parts.words: One is far away to have this the day before
parts.note: someone whose mind is far away is having a reverie, and putting the word day before this word names that reverie

explanation.walkthrough: 'the day before' looks like yesterday, but it means placing DAY in front of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Put day before it and you have a reverie, the state of someone whose thoughts are far away.

clue.text: Crook ran home with candlestick

indicators.note: crook means bent or twisted, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A thief ran home with a candlestick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crook' looks like a thief but rearranges RAN HOME.
explanation.definitionFit: A seven-branched Jewish candelabrum.

clue.text: Second to none country bandmaster

parts.note: O looks like zero, none
the USA is a country

explanation.surface: A bandleader who is second to none in his country.
explanation.walkthrough: John Philip Sousa was the American bandmaster famous for marches.
explanation.definitionFit: John Philip Sousa, the American March King, led the US Marine Band.

clue.text: German diver prohibited to come up about nothing

indicators.note: about means the reversed word goes around the letter for nothing
in a down clue, coming up means reading upwards, reversed

parts.note: tabu is a variant spelling of taboo, prohibited
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A German swimmer banned from surfacing for no reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to come up' reads TABU upwards as UBAT, since this is a down clue, and 'about' has that word go around O.
explanation.definitionFit: A German submarine, which dives under water.

clue.text: Main street Arab, a prickly sort

parts.note: the main is an old word for the sea
an old term for a ragged homeless child, a guttersnipe

explanation.surface: A rough ragamuffin on the high street is a thorny character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main street' looks like a town's high street, but the main is the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiny marine creature, covered with sharp quills.

clue.text: A great many appear in this spectacle

definitions.meaning: a great deal or many, informally

explanation.surface: Crowds turning up for a show.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally a lot or a great deal; also a view or something to see.

clue.text: "The sly shade of a --'Dean" (Brooke)

parts.note: a line from Rupert Brooke's poem Grantchester, completed by a word meaning of the countryside

explanation.definitionFit: Brooke's Grantchester speaks of a country dean's ghost; the missing word means of the countryside.

clue.text: Chance of success for fighter's comeback is improving

parts.note: a look-in is a chance of success

indicators.note: comeback signals the boxer's word is read the other way round

parts.note: a pug is a boxer, from pugilist

explanation.surface: A boxer's comeback improves his odds of winning.
explanation.walkthrough: A look-in is British informal for a chance; 'comeback' reverses the boxer, a pug being short for pugilist.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting better, as when things are said to be on the up.

clue.text: Sprinter takes one run at either end

indicators.note: takes means the run letters hold the word for one
at either end means the run letter appears at the start and the finish

parts.note: r is the cricket abbreviation for run
an ace is a one on dice or cards

explanation.surface: A sprinter runs one race, with a dash at the start and finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at either end' puts R (run) on both sides, and 'takes' puts ACE (one) between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast runner, someone who competes in speed events.

clue.text: Where to shelter from bugle call

definitions.meaning: the military signal sounded at sunset

explanation.surface: A soldier hears the bugle and looks for cover.
explanation.definitionFit: A hideaway refuge; also the sunset military signal sounded on a bugle.

clue.text: Biblical hair remover

parts.note: a woman in the Book of Judges who had Samson's hair cut, robbing him of his strength

explanation.definitionFit: In Judges she betrayed Samson by having his locks shorn.
